text: This lab is a hand trace, not a circuit build — you'll walk through the exact arithmetic Shor's algorithm's classical post-processing performs, for the same N equals 15 used throughout this chapter, with two different choices of a. One succeeds cleanly. One fails cleanly. Both outcomes are correct behavior.

First, a equals 7. The powers of 7 mod 15 are 7, 4, 13, then 1 at the fourth power, so r equals 4, which is even. A to the r over 2 mod N is 7 squared mod 15, which is 4 — and since 4 doesn't equal negative 1 mod 15, which is 14, the condition for success holds. The two gcds come out to 3 and 5, both nontrivial, and 3 times 5 is 15. Every step succeeded exactly as the proof predicts.

Now a equals 14. The powers are 14, then 196 mod 15 equals 1 — so r equals 2 already, which is even. A to the r over 2 mod N is 14 to the first power mod 15, which is 14. And 14 is exactly negative 1 mod 15 — the failure condition Lesson 21 flagged. Computing the gcds anyway: gcd of 13 and 15 is 1, and gcd of 15 and 15 is 15 — both trivial. No factor at all, even though every individual step was computed correctly.

The correct response to a failure like this isn't to debug the algorithm — the arithmetic is exactly right, this is precisely the predicted failure mode. The correct response is simply to discard this a, pick a new random one, and retry — the proven probability of at least one-half per attempt means a second try usually resolves it. A real quantum run behaves exactly the same way, measuring a result consistent with r equals 2 just as validly as any other outcome. And notice this entire lab needed only a handful of modular multiplications on numbers smaller than 20 — N equals 15 is trivial on purpose, to make the logic inspectable; RSA-2048 is the case that actually needs thousands of qubits.
Chapter 6 turns to other landmark quantum algorithms beyond Grover's and Shor's, starting with the Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm.
